questions.title: Which of the following is not a cause of metabolic acidosis
questions.question: Which of the following is not a cause of metabolic acidosis:

explanations.A: Correct. Vomiting empties the stomach of hydrochloric acid, and the resulting loss of hydrogen ion, together with the renal contraction-alkalosis response to the accompanying volume depletion, drives the blood toward metabolic alkalosis rather than acidosis. This is the opposite direction from every other option listed, each of which is a genuine cause of metabolic acidosis. Because vomiting is therefore not a cause of metabolic acidosis, it is the correct answer to this 'which is NOT a cause' question.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Strenuous muscular exercise generates lactic acid faster than it can be cleared, producing lactic acidosis, a recognised cause of metabolic acidosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diarrhoea washes bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid out of the body, producing a normal-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Failing kidneys cannot excrete the daily fixed-acid load or reclaim filtered bicarbonate normally, so retained acid produces metabolic acidosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Accumulating ketoacids (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) in uncontrolled diabetes or starvation is a classic high-anion-gap cause of metabolic acidosis.

questions.learning_objective: Which of the following is not a cause of metabolic acidosis

questions.title: Inhibition of respiration as a feature of an acid-base disturbance
questions.question: Inhibition of respiration is a feature of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Respiratory acidosis is itself caused by hypoventilation (inhibited respiration is the primary problem, not a compensatory feature).
explanations.B: Incorrect. A primary respiratory acidosis is compensated by the kidney retaining bicarbonate, not by any further change in ventilation.
explanations.C: Correct. Metabolic alkalosis (raised pH and raised bicarbonate) is compensated by the respiratory centre reducing ventilation rate and depth -- hypoventilation, i.e. inhibition of respiration -- which retains carbon dioxide. The retained CO2 raises carbonic acid and hydrogen ion concentration, pulling the pH back toward normal without correcting the underlying bicarbonate excess. This hypoventilatory response is exactly why compensated metabolic alkalosis, among the five options, is the one in which inhibited respiration is a defining feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis is compensated by increased, not inhibited, ventilation (hyperventilation blowing off CO2).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis is the primary disturbance itself, before any respiratory response has occurred; the inhibited-respiration compensation only becomes a feature once compensation is under way.

questions.learning_objective: Inhibition of respiration as a feature of an acid-base disturbance

questions.title: True statement regarding sodium chloride solution
questions.question: Which of the following is True regarding sodium chloride solution.

options.A: Solute particles are more than 200 nm in diameter
options.D: Can be seen by ordinary microscope
options.E: Solute particles range between 1-200 nm in diameter

explanations.A: Incorrect. Particles more than roughly 200 nanometres in diameter describe a coarse suspension, not a true solution such as sodium chloride, and are large enough to be visible and to settle out rather than remain dissolved.
explanations.B: Correct. Sodium chloride dissolves into hydrated ions under about 1 nanometre in diameter -- so small that, unlike colloidal particles, they pass freely through both filter paper and a semipermeable (dialysis) membrane. This free passage through a semipermeable membrane is exactly the property used to define a true (crystalloid) solution and to separate it experimentally from a colloid, whose larger particles are retained by such a membrane even though they still pass filter paper. Being able to cross a semipermeable membrane is therefore the single defining physical property that makes sodium chloride solution a true solution rather than a colloid or suspension.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Filter paper retains only the coarsest suspension particles; a true solution such as sodium chloride passes through filter paper just as freely as it passes through a semipermeable membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dissolved sodium and chloride ions are far too small to be resolved by an ordinary light microscope, which can only visualise particles down to roughly the size of a bacterium or larger.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A particle diameter of roughly 1-200 nanometres is the classic range given for a colloid, not a true solution; true-solution particles such as dissolved Na+ and Cl- are smaller than about 1 nanometre.

questions.learning_objective: True statement regarding sodium chloride solution

questions.title: Carbohydrate with no nutritional value
questions.question: Which out of the following is a carbohydrate with no nutritional value?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glycogen is joined by alpha-1,4 (with alpha-1,6 branch) glycosidic bonds, which human amylase readily hydrolyses to glucose, giving it full nutritional value as the body's own storage carbohydrate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Starch's alpha-1,4/alpha-1,6 bonds are digested by salivary and pancreatic amylase into absorbable glucose, making it a major dietary source of calories.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dextrins are partial amylase-digestion products of starch, still built of alpha-linked glucose and further digested to glucose, so they retain nutritional value.
explanations.D: Correct. Cellulose is built from D-glucose units joined exclusively by beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds, and humans lack the cellulase enzyme needed to hydrolyse that bond. Because it passes through the human gastrointestinal tract completely undigested, cellulose yields no absorbable monosaccharide and therefore contributes no calories or nutritional value, unlike starch and glycogen, whose alpha-linked bonds are cleaved efficiently by human amylase. Cellulose instead functions in the human diet purely as insoluble dietary fibre, adding bulk and aiding transit rather than being absorbed as a nutrient.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lactose is digested by lactase (in those who express it) into absorbable galactose and glucose, giving it nutritional value.

questions.title: Epimer of glucose
questions.question: Epimer of glucose is

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fructose shares glucose's molecular formula but differs in functional group (ketone vs aldehyde), making it glucose's aldose-ketose isomer, not an epimer.
explanations.B: Correct. Mannose and glucose share the same molecular formula and differ in configuration only at carbon 2, making mannose the C2 epimer of glucose -- the same kind of single-carbon relationship by which galactose is glucose's C4 epimer. An epimer is defined precisely by this one-carbon difference at a non-anomeric position, distinguishing it from an anomer (differs only at the anomeric carbon) or an aldose-ketose isomer (differs in functional group, like fructose). Mannose is therefore the correct answer because it is the specific sugar related to glucose by exactly this one-carbon epimeric relationship.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ribose is a five-carbon aldopentose, a different chain length from six-carbon glucose, so the epimer relationship (which requires the same molecular formula) does not apply.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glyceraldehyde is the simplest three-carbon aldose, far shorter than six-carbon glucose, so it cannot be an epimer of it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Xylose is a five-carbon aldopentose, a different chain length from glucose, so it is not an epimer of glucose.

questions.title: Enzyme stimulated by heparin
questions.question: . . . . . . . stimulates lipoprotein lipase enzyme

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inulin is a plant fructan storage polysaccharide used clinically to measure glomerular filtration rate; it has no lipoprotein lipase-releasing action.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyaluronic acid is the one unsulfated glycosaminoglycan, dominant in synovial fluid and vitreous humour; it plays no role in releasing lipoprotein lipase.
explanations.C: Correct. Heparin, beyond its well-known anticoagulant action, displaces lipoprotein lipase from its endothelial heparan-sulfate binding sites into the circulating plasma, activating it to hydrolyse the triglycerides carried in chylomicrons and VLDL. This heparin-releasable pool of lipoprotein lipase is the basis of the historical 'post-heparin lipolytic activity' assay once used to measure the enzyme clinically. Heparin is therefore the correct answer among the glycosaminoglycans listed, since none of the others shares this specific lipoprotein lipase-releasing action.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Keratan sulfate is concentrated in the cornea and cartilage; it has no described role in stimulating lipoprotein lipase.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Dermatan sulphate is a structural glycosaminoglycan of skin and blood vessels; it does not stimulate lipoprotein lipase.

questions.title: Gradual change in specific rotation of a sugar solution
questions.question: . . . . . . . is gradual change in specific rotation of optical active substance when for a time.

explanations.A: Correct. Mutarotation is the slow, spontaneous change in optical rotation shown by a freshly dissolved reducing sugar as its open-chain form cyclises and interconverts between the alpha and beta anomeric ring forms until an equilibrium mixture is reached. This is exactly the gradual, time-dependent change in specific rotation the question describes, distinguishing mutarotation from optical activity in general (which is present throughout, not a changing property) and from racemisation (formation of an equal D/L mixture, a different phenomenon). Mutarotation is therefore the correct term for this specific gradual equilibration process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Optical activity is simply the general property of rotating plane-polarised light; it does not itself describe a gradual change over time.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Isomerism is a structural relationship between two different compounds, not a time-dependent change within one dissolved compound.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sugar reducing power refers to a free anomeric hydroxyl's ability to reduce an oxidising agent (as in Benedict's test), an unrelated chemical property.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A racemic mixture is an equal mixture of D and L enantiomers with zero net optical rotation, a static end-state rather than the gradual process being described.

questions.learning_objective: Gradual change in specific rotation of a sugar solution

questions.title: Tissue rich in keratan sulphate
questions.question: Keratan sulphate is found in abundance in

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heart muscle is not a characteristic site of keratan sulphate concentration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The liver is not a characteristic site of keratan sulphate concentration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The adrenal cortex is a steroid-hormone-producing tissue, not a site characteristically rich in keratan sulphate.
explanations.D: Correct. Keratan sulphate is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan present at particularly high concentration in the cornea, where its precisely regular spacing between collagen fibrils is thought to contribute to corneal transparency. It is also found in cartilage and intervertebral discs, but the cornea is its most exam-characteristic and clinically recognised location. This distinguishes keratan sulphate from the other named glycosaminoglycans, none of which is specifically associated with the cornea in the way keratan sulphate is.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The adrenal medulla, which secretes catecholamines, is not a characteristic site of keratan sulphate concentration.

questions.title: Classification of ribulose
questions.question: Ribulose is

explanations.A: Incorrect. A ketotetrose has four carbons, not five; erythrulose, not ribulose, is the four-carbon ketose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An aldopentose carries an aldehyde group; ribulose carries a ketone group, so it is a ketose, not an aldose.
explanations.C: Correct. Ribulose is a five-carbon monosaccharide carrying a ketone functional group, making it a ketopentose -- a key intermediate of the pentose phosphate pathway. This term combines its carbon count (five, a pentose) with its functional group (ketone, a ketose) into a single classification, correctly distinguishing it from an aldopentose such as ribose (its aldose isomer at the same chain length) and from a tetrose or hexose sugar of a different chain length. Ribulose is therefore correctly classed as a ketopentose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An aldopentose carries an aldehyde group at C1; ribulose's ketone group at C2 makes it a ketopentose instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A ketohexose has six carbons; ribulose has five, making it a ketopentose, not a ketohexose.

questions.title: Product not formed by glucose oxidation
questions.question: Glucose on oxidation does not give

explanations.A: Correct. Oxidising glucose at different carbons yields distinct acids -- gluconic acid (C1 oxidised), glucuronic acid (C6 oxidised) and glucosaccharic (glucaric) acid (both C1 and C6 oxidised) -- but a glycoside is not among them. Glycosides instead form by an entirely different reaction: condensation of the anomeric (C1) hydroxyl with an alcohol or other -OH-bearing group, releasing water, not by any oxidation step. Because glycoside formation is a condensation reaction rather than an oxidation, glucose oxidation does not give a glycoside, making this the correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucosaccharic (glucaric) acid is formed by oxidising both the C1 aldehyde and the C6 hydroxyl of glucose, so it is a genuine glucose-oxidation product.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucuronic acid is formed by oxidising the C6 hydroxyl of glucose to a carboxylic acid, so it is a genuine glucose-oxidation product.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Iduronic acid, while not formed by a single direct oxidation of glucose, is grouped with the other listed oxidation-pathway-related uronic acid derivatives in this exam item; the printed key identifies glycoside, formed by condensation rather than any oxidative chemistry, as the one true non-oxidation product among the five options.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Gluconic acid is formed by oxidising the C1 aldehyde of glucose to a carboxylic acid, so it is a genuine glucose-oxidation product.

questions.learning_objective: Product not formed by glucose oxidation

questions.title: Relationship between alpha- and beta-D-glucose
questions.question: alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-glucose are

explanations.A: Incorrect. 'Epimers' is the broader term for sugars differing at any one specified non-anomeric carbon; alpha/beta-D-glucose differ specifically at the anomeric carbon, which is the narrower, more precise term 'anomers'.
explanations.B: Correct. When open-chain D-glucose cyclises, a new stereocentre is created at C1, the anomeric carbon; the two possible configurations there, alpha and beta, are called anomers -- a special case of epimerism restricted specifically to the anomeric carbon and produced by ring closure rather than by any other chemical change. Because alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-glucose differ only at this one anomeric carbon, they are correctly and specifically called anomers rather than the broader term epimers. Anomers is therefore the precise, correct classification for this pair.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both alpha- and beta-D-glucose are aldoses (retain the same C1 aldehyde-derived hemiacetal); aldo-keto isomerism describes a functional-group difference such as glucose vs fructose, not this pair.
explanations.D: Incorrect. D and L isomers are mirror images differing in configuration at the highest-numbered chiral carbon (C5 in glucose), not at the anomeric carbon; both forms here are D-glucose.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pyranose and furanose describe ring size (six-membered vs five-membered), not the anomeric configuration; both alpha- and beta-D-glucose are drawn here as the same (pyranose) ring size.

questions.title: Disaccharide with an alpha 1-to-2 glycosidic linkage
questions.question: The monosaccharide units are linked by alpha 1->2 glycosidic linkage in

explanations.A: Incorrect. Maltose is two glucose units joined by an alpha-1,4-glycosidic bond, not 1,2.
explanations.B: Correct. Sucrose is formed from alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-fructose joined head-to-head through both of their anomeric carbons (glucose C1 to fructose C2), a bond described as an alpha-1,2-glycosidic linkage. Because both anomeric carbons are tied up in this bond, sucrose has no free reducing end and is a non-reducing sugar, unlike maltose or lactose, which each leave one anomeric carbon free. Sucrose is therefore the correct answer as the disaccharide specifically joined by this 1,2 linkage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mannose is a monosaccharide, not a disaccharide, so it has no glycosidic linkage at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lactose is galactose and glucose joined by a beta-1,4-glycosidic bond, not an alpha-1,2 bond.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Starch's glucose units are joined by alpha-1,4 backbone bonds (with alpha-1,6 branches in amylopectin), not alpha-1,2.

questions.learning_objective: Disaccharide with an alpha 1-to-2 glycosidic linkage

questions.title: Factor that enhances rancidity
questions.question: Which of the following can enhance rancidity?

explanations.A: Correct. Rancidity is the oxidative spoilage of fats, driven by a free-radical chain reaction in which a radical abstracts a hydrogen from an unsaturated fatty acid, forming a lipid radical that reacts with oxygen and propagates further radical formation. This self-propagating chain is exactly what enhances and accelerates rancidity once initiated. Because every other option listed instead protects against rancidity, free radicals are the correct answer as the enhancing factor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Antioxidants (such as phenolic compounds and vitamin E) quench free radicals and interrupt the chain reaction, protecting against rancidity rather than enhancing it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Avoiding air (oxygen) exposure removes a reactant the free-radical chain reaction needs, protecting against rancidity rather than enhancing it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phenols are a classic chemical class of antioxidant, protecting against rancidity rather than enhancing it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Avoiding bacteria removes a source of lipase enzymes that can initiate fat spoilage, protecting against rancidity rather than enhancing it.

questions.title: Phospholipid that acts as lung surfactant
questions.question: Phospholipid acting as lung surfactant is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cephalin (phosphatidylethanolamine) is a general structural membrane phospholipid, not the principal pulmonary surfactant.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Phosphatidylinositol is chiefly a membrane signalling lipid (precursor of second messengers), not the principal pulmonary surfactant.
explanations.C: Correct. Lecithin, specifically dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), is the major phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant, secreted by type II pneumocytes to lower alveolar surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse at end-expiration. The other phospholipids listed are structural or signalling membrane lipids rather than the principal surfactant component, which is why lecithin is specifically the one associated with lung surfactant function. Lecithin is therefore the correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phosphatidylserine is a structural membrane phospholipid best known for its role as an 'eat-me' signal when externalised in apoptosis, not as lung surfactant.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sphingomyelin is a sphingosine-based membrane phospholipid important in myelin, not the principal pulmonary surfactant.

questions.learning_objective: Phospholipid that acts as lung surfactant

questions.title: Structural formula of arachidonic acid
questions.question: Structure of arachidonic acid is

explanations.A: Incorrect. C18:2, Delta-9,12 is linoleic acid, arachidonic acid's essential-fatty-acid precursor, not arachidonic acid itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C18:3, Delta-9,12,15 is alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 essential fatty acid, not arachidonic acid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. C16, Delta-9 (palmitoleic acid) is a sixteen-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid, far shorter and less unsaturated than arachidonic acid.
explanations.D: Correct. Arachidonic acid is written C20:4, Delta-5,8,11,14 -- a twenty-carbon polyunsaturated (omega-6) fatty acid with four cis double bonds at carbons 5, 8, 11 and 14, derived from linoleic acid. It serves as the direct precursor for the eicosanoid signalling molecules (prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes), released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. This specific twenty-carbon, four-double-bond formula is what identifies arachidonic acid among the fatty acids listed.
explanations.E: Incorrect. As with option C, C16, Delta-9 (palmitoleic acid) is a sixteen-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid, not arachidonic acid.

questions.title: Components of a ganglioside
questions.question: What are the components of Gangliosides?

options.B: Glycerol + Fatty acids + Phosphoric acid + Galactose
options.C: Glycerol + Fatty acids + Phosphoric acid + Nitrogenous base + Galactose
options.D: Sphingosine + fatty acids + Phosphoric acid + Galactose
options.E: Sphingosine + fatty acids + Glucose + Galactose + Sialic acid

explanations.A: Incorrect. This omits both glucose and the sialic acid that specifically defines a ganglioside; sphingosine + fatty acid + galactose alone describes a simpler glycosphingolipid, such as a cerebroside, not a ganglioside.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This glycerol/phosphoric-acid-based composition instead describes a glycerophospholipid, not a sphingosine-based glycosphingolipid such as a ganglioside.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This glycerol/phosphoric-acid/nitrogenous-base composition describes a glycerophospholipid (such as lecithin), an entirely different lipid family from the sphingosine-based ganglioside.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gangliosides are not built on a phosphoric-acid backbone; that is a feature of the glycerophospholipids, not the glycosphingolipids.
explanations.E: Correct. Gangliosides are the most complex glycosphingolipids, built on a ceramide backbone (sphingosine condensed with a fatty acid) to which an oligosaccharide chain -- typically including glucose, galactose and one or more sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) residues -- is attached. The presence of sialic acid is exactly what distinguishes a ganglioside from a simpler glycosphingolipid such as a cerebroside, which carries only a single neutral sugar and no sialic acid. This sphingosine + fatty acid + glucose + galactose + sialic acid combination is therefore the correct ganglioside composition.

questions.title: Lipid that is not a steroid
questions.question: Which of the following is not steroid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A sterol (such as cholesterol) shares the four-ring steroid nucleus and is a true steroid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bile acids are synthesised from cholesterol and retain the steroid ring nucleus, making them true steroids.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Oestrogen is a steroid hormone, built on the same four-ring steroid nucleus as cholesterol.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucocorticoids (such as cortisol) are adrenal steroid hormones, sharing the same steroid ring nucleus.
explanations.E: Correct. Beta carotene is an isoprenoid/carotenoid pigment (a vitamin A precursor) built from isoprene units, not the fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus that defines a steroid. Sterols, bile acids, oestrogen and glucocorticoids all share that steroid nucleus and are therefore true steroids, unlike beta carotene, which belongs to an entirely different lipid class. Beta carotene is therefore correctly identified as the one non-steroid among the five options.

questions.learning_objective: Lipid that is not a steroid

questions.title: Feature of the quaternary structure of proteins
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the quaternary structure of proteins?

options.D: Relative positions of amino, groups, and R

explanations.A: Correct. Quaternary structure is the level of protein organisation formed when two or more separate polypeptide chains (subunits) assemble into one functional multi-chain protein -- a protein built of a single chain has primary, secondary and tertiary structure only, while a protein such as haemoglobin, built of multiple chains, adds this quaternary level for its full activity. This combination-of-subunits description is exactly what quaternary structure means, correctly distinguishing it from secondary structure (alpha-helix/beta-sheet, a single-chain backbone folding pattern) and from primary structure (the amino acid sequence itself).
explanations.B: Incorrect. The alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet are examples of secondary structure, a single-chain local folding pattern, not quaternary structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The 'skeleton of amino acids' describes the primary structure (the linear amino-acid sequence), not the multi-subunit quaternary level.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The relative positions of the amino and R groups along a single chain describe primary/tertiary-level detail, not the assembly of separate subunits that defines quaternary structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Side-chain orientation and position describe tertiary structure (the 3D fold of one chain), not the multi-chain assembly that defines quaternary structure.

questions.learning_objective: Feature of the quaternary structure of proteins

questions.title: Non-essential amino acid
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-essential amino acid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Threonine is one of the nine essential amino acids and must come from the diet.
explanations.B: Correct. An essential amino acid cannot be synthesised by the body in sufficient quantity and must come from the diet; glutamine, by contrast, is readily synthesised from glutamic acid by amidation and is therefore classed as non-essential. Threonine, phenylalanine, valine and lysine, the other four options, are each among the nine amino acids the body cannot synthesise and so must obtain from food. Glutamine is therefore correctly identified as the non-essential amino acid among these five options.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid and must come from the diet.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Valine is a branched-chain essential amino acid and must come from the diet.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lysine is one of the nine essential amino acids and must come from the diet.

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p6

questions.title: Neutral amino acid
questions.question: Which of the following is a neutral amino acid?

explanations.A: Correct. Amino acids are grouped by their side-chain charge at physiological pH into acidic, basic and neutral (uncharged side chain) classes. Glycine's side chain is simply a hydrogen atom, carrying no ionisable charge, which makes it the simplest and most straightforward example of a neutral amino acid. This is why glycine, and none of the other four listed amino acids, is correctly classed as neutral.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysine carries a basic (positively charged) side-chain amino group at physiological pH, making it a basic, not neutral, amino acid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Arginine carries a basic (positively charged) side-chain guanidino group at physiological pH, making it a basic, not neutral, amino acid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Histidine carries a side-chain imidazole group that is basic (partially protonated near physiological pH), making it a basic, not neutral, amino acid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Glutamate carries an acidic (negatively charged) side-chain carboxyl group at physiological pH, making it an acidic, not neutral, amino acid.

questions.title: Classification of cysteine
questions.question: Cysteine is a/an . . . . . . amino acid.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cysteine's side chain is a neutral thiol group, not an acidic carboxyl group; it is not classed as acidic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cysteine is a non-essential amino acid (synthesised from methionine and serine via the transsulfuration pathway), not an essential one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cysteine's side chain has no aromatic ring; phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan are the aromatic amino acids.
explanations.D: Correct. Cysteine carries a thiol (-SH) side chain, making it, together with methionine, one of the two sulphur-containing amino acids. Its thiol group allows two cysteine residues to form a covalent disulfide bond, a major stabiliser of tertiary and quaternary protein structure. This defining sulphur-containing side chain is what correctly classifies cysteine among the five options given.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cysteine's side chain is a neutral thiol group, not a basic amino or guanidino group; it is not classed as basic.

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p7

questions.title: Consequences of protein denaturation
questions.question: Denaturation of protein:

options.A: Disrupts the primary or secondary or tertiary structure of protein
options.B: Disrupts the secondary and tertiary structure only
options.C: Disrupts all the primary, secondary and tertiary and even quaternary structure of protein.
options.D: Will not affect the original biological activity

explanations.A: Incorrect. Denaturation specifically spares the primary structure -- the peptide bonds holding the amino-acid sequence together are not broken -- so 'disrupts the primary ... structure' is not correct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Denaturation disrupts secondary, tertiary and, where present, quaternary structure together, not secondary and tertiary alone to the exclusion of quaternary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Denaturation does not disrupt the primary structure; the peptide-bond sequence remains intact even as the higher-order folding is lost.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Denaturation characteristically abolishes a protein's original biological activity (for example, enzymatic activity), since that activity depends on the native higher-order fold.
explanations.E: Correct. Denaturation ruptures the bonds holding secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, leaving the primary sequence intact but the protein insoluble, more viscous, more digestible and biologically dead. None of the four preceding options states this correctly: option A wrongly includes the primary structure, option B wrongly excludes quaternary structure, option C wrongly includes the primary structure, and option D wrongly claims biological activity is preserved. Because none of them accurately describes denaturation, 'none of the above' is the correct answer.

questions.title: Protein with a high length-to-width ratio
questions.question: Which protein of the given has a length:width ratio > 10?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haemoglobin is a compact, roughly spherical globular protein, with a length-to-width ratio close to 1, not above 10.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Myoglobin is a compact, roughly spherical globular protein, with a length-to-width ratio close to 1, not above 10.
explanations.C: Correct. Proteins are broadly classed by shape into fibrous (elongated, length-to-width ratio greater than about 10, e.g. fibrin/fibrinogen, collagen, keratin) and globular (compact, roughly spherical, ratio close to 1). Fibrin's elongated polymer strands, formed when thrombin cleaves fibrinogen and the resulting monomers polymerise into long fibres, are the classic example of a fibrous protein with exactly this high length-to-width ratio. Fibrin is therefore the correct answer among the five proteins listed, the other four all being globular.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Albumin is a compact, roughly spherical globular plasma protein, with a length-to-width ratio close to 1, not above 10.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Globulins are compact, roughly spherical globular proteins, with a length-to-width ratio close to 1, not above 10.

questions.learning_objective: Protein with a high length-to-width ratio

questions.title: Functional character of the sympathetic nervous system
questions.question: Regarding the autonomic nervous system:

options.A: The sympathetic system is catabolic (energy consuming)
options.B: Parasympathetic acts as a one unit in stresses
options.C: Sympathetic system arises from some cranial nerves and few sacral segments

explanations.A: Correct. The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system is functionally catabolic: its 'fight-or-flight' discharge mobilises stored energy by stimulating glycogenolysis and lipolysis and by increasing cardiac output and ventilation, preparing the body for vigorous activity. This energy-mobilising, energy-consuming character is the defining functional contrast with the parasympathetic ('rest and digest', energy-conserving/anabolic) division. Because this catabolic description is accurate and matches standard physiology teaching, it is the correct answer among the options given.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the sympathetic system, not the parasympathetic, that tends to discharge as one coordinated mass response during stress ('mass action'); the parasympathetic system typically acts in a more discrete, localised fashion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is the parasympathetic (not sympathetic) system that arises from certain cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, X) and the sacral segments (S2-S4); the sympathetic system arises instead from the thoracolumbar (T1-L2) spinal segments.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is parasympathetic, not sympathetic, ganglia that are typically terminal (located close to or within the target organ); sympathetic ganglia are typically paravertebral/prevertebral, relatively close to the spinal cord.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option A correctly describes the sympathetic system as catabolic, so 'none of the above' is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: Functional character of the sympathetic nervous system

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p8

questions.title: Organisation of the autonomic nervous system
questions.question: The autonomic nervous system:

options.B: Is an efferent two neuronal system
options.C: Is a part of the central nervous system
options.D: Has a wider outflow than the somatic nervous system

explanations.A: Incorrect. Voluntary movement is controlled by the somatic motor system, not the autonomic nervous system, which instead controls involuntary functions (viscera, glands, smooth and cardiac muscle).
explanations.B: Correct. Every autonomic motor pathway, sympathetic or parasympathetic, uses two neurons in series -- a preganglionic neuron synapsing in a peripheral ganglion onto a postganglionic neuron that reaches the target organ. This two-neuron efferent arrangement contrasts directly with the somatic motor pathway, which reaches skeletal muscle via a single motor neuron with no intervening peripheral ganglion. This defining efferent two-neuron organisation is why option B is the correct answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The autonomic nervous system has its preganglionic cell bodies within the CNS but its ganglia and postganglionic neurons lie in the peripheral nervous system; it is not itself part of the CNS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the somatic nervous system that has the wider, more discretely targeted motor outflow to individual skeletal muscles; the autonomic system's outflow is comparatively more diffuse to viscera rather than 'wider' in the sense implied here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since option A is false (voluntary movement is somatic, not autonomic), 'all of the above' cannot be correct.

questions.learning_objective: Organisation of the autonomic nervous system

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p8

questions.title: Definition of an autonomic ganglion
questions.question: The autonomic ganglia

options.B: Have chemical transmitters either acetycholine or noradrenaline
options.C: Its lateral type may be parasympathetic
options.D: collection of nerve cells outside CNS

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomic ganglia lie in the peripheral nervous system, outside the CNS, not inside it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ganglionic synapse itself (preganglionic to postganglionic neuron) uses acetylcholine in both sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions; noradrenaline is instead the transmitter released at most sympathetic postganglionic-to-target-organ synapses, not within the ganglion itself, so this statement mischaracterises ganglionic transmission specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 'Lateral' ganglia (the paravertebral sympathetic chain) are specifically sympathetic in type, not potentially parasympathetic.
explanations.D: Correct. An autonomic ganglion is, by definition, a collection of neuronal cell bodies lying outside the central nervous system, where preganglionic fibres synapse onto postganglionic neurons using acetylcholine as the ganglionic neurotransmitter. Sympathetic ganglia are typically paravertebral or prevertebral, relatively close to the spinal cord, while parasympathetic ganglia typically lie close to or within the wall of the target organ, but both share this basic definition of being a peripheral (outside-CNS) collection of nerve cell bodies. This is exactly why 'collection of nerve cells outside CNS' is the correct, defining answer.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option D correctly defines an autonomic ganglion, so 'none of the above' is not correct.

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p8

questions.title: Effect of sympathetic stimulation on the eye
questions.question: Stimulation of sympathetic supply produces:

explanations.A: Correct. Sympathetic stimulation contracts the radially arranged dilator pupillae muscle of the iris, producing mydriasis (pupillary dilatation) -- part of the classic 'fight-or-flight' response that widens the visual field. This is the opposite of parasympathetic-mediated contraction of the circularly arranged constrictor (sphincter) pupillae muscle, which produces miosis. Mydriasis is therefore the correct direct effect of sympathetic stimulation on the eye.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ciliary muscle contraction mediates accommodation (near vision) and is a parasympathetic, not sympathetic, action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dropping of the upper eyelid (ptosis) results from loss of sympathetic tone to the superior tarsal muscle, as in Horner's syndrome, not from active sympathetic stimulation; active sympathetic stimulation instead helps elevate the eyelid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation typically produces vasoconstriction (via alpha receptors) in most vascular beds including conjunctival vessels, not vasodilatation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation increases, not decreases, sweat gland secretion, via the atypical cholinergic sympathetic innervation of sweat glands.

questions.learning_objective: Effect of sympathetic stimulation on the eye

questions.title: Organ without sympathetic supply
questions.question: The following organs have sympathetic supply, except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sweat glands do receive sympathetic innervation (atypically cholinergic), so this is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Blood vessels of skeletal muscle receive sympathetic vasomotor innervation (both vasoconstrictor alpha and vasodilator beta-2/cholinergic fibres), so this is not the exception.
explanations.C: Correct. Almost every peripheral organ, including sweat glands, skeletal-muscle blood vessels, cardiac (ventricular) muscle and bronchial smooth muscle, receives sympathetic innervation. The constrictor (sphincter) pupillae muscle is a notable exception, receiving parasympathetic innervation only, via the oculomotor nerve and ciliary ganglion, with no direct sympathetic supply. This makes constrictor pupillae the correct exception among the five structures listed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ventricular (cardiac) muscle receives sympathetic innervation, increasing heart rate and contractility, so this is not the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bronchial smooth muscle receives sympathetic innervation (functionally via circulating adrenaline on beta-2 receptors), so this is not the exception.

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p9

questions.title: Effect of sympathetic stimulation on the airway
questions.question: Sympathetic stimulation results in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation produces pupillary dilatation (mydriasis), not constriction, which is instead a parasympathetic effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ciliary muscle contraction (accommodation) is a parasympathetic, not sympathetic, action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation increases, not decreases, sweat secretion.
explanations.D: Correct. Circulating adrenaline and sympathetic activation relax bronchial smooth muscle via beta-2 adrenergic receptors, producing bronchodilatation and increased airway calibre -- the physiological basis for using beta-2 agonists such as salbutamol as bronchodilator drugs. This is the opposite of the bronchoconstriction produced by parasympathetic (muscarinic) stimulation. Bronchodilatation is therefore the correct sympathetic-stimulation effect among the options listed.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Micturition (bladder emptying) is promoted by parasympathetic stimulation (detrusor contraction); sympathetic stimulation instead favours bladder filling/storage.

questions.learning_objective: Effect of sympathetic stimulation on the airway

questions.title: Nature of the greater splanchnic nerve
questions.question: The greater splanchnic nerve:

options.B: Increase contraction of wall of gastrointestinal tract and inhibits its sphincters
options.C: Decreases glycogenolysis and fibrinogen formation from the liver

explanations.A: Correct. The greater splanchnic nerve is formed from preganglionic sympathetic fibres (roughly T5-T9) that pass through the sympathetic chain without synapsing and travel to the coeliac ganglion, where they synapse on postganglionic neurons supplying the abdominal viscera. It is a purely sympathetic structure, carrying no parasympathetic fibres, which is why 'belongs to sympathetic system' is the direct, correct description of it, unlike the other options, each of which misstates one of its actual (opposite-direction) effects.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sympathetic (splanchnic) stimulation decreases gastrointestinal motility and contracts, rather than inhibits, the sphincters -- the reverse of what this option states, which instead describes a parasympathetic effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation increases, not decreases, hepatic glycogenolysis (mobilising glucose for a stress response); it does not selectively decrease fibrinogen formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While sympathetic activity does produce bronchodilatation, that effect is not carried by the greater splanchnic nerve, which instead supplies the abdominal viscera via the coeliac ganglion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is the direct cardiac sympathetic (cardiac accelerator) nerves, not the greater splanchnic nerve (which targets abdominal viscera), that increase cardiac rate, contractility and conduction.

questions.learning_objective: Nature of the greater splanchnic nerve

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p9

questions.title: Relay site of T1-T2 preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head and neck
questions.question: Preganglionic neurons arise from the lateral horn cells of the first and second thoracic segments:

options.A: Carry parasympathetic supply to the head and neck
options.B: End in terminal ganglia in effector organs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibres from the lateral horn of the thoracic cord are sympathetic (thoracolumbar outflow) by definition, not parasympathetic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Terminal ganglia located within or close to the effector organ are a parasympathetic pattern; these T1-T2 sympathetic preganglionic fibres instead relay in the relatively distant cervical sympathetic ganglia.
explanations.C: Correct. Preganglionic sympathetic neurons supplying the head and neck arise from the lateral horn of the upper one or two thoracic spinal cord segments (T1-T2), ascend the sympathetic chain, and synapse in one of the cervical sympathetic ganglia (superior, middle or inferior/stellate). Postganglionic fibres from there follow the carotid arteries and cranial nerves to their targets in the head and neck, including the pupil dilator, tarsal muscles, sweat glands and blood vessels. This relay in the cervical ganglia is exactly what makes option C the correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased cardiac contractility is produced by sympathetic fibres reaching the heart via the cardiac plexus, a separate pathway from the T1-T2 fibres supplying the head and neck described here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation causes bronchodilatation, not bronchoconstriction, and in any case that effect is carried by fibres reaching the lungs, not by these head-and-neck-directed T1-T2 fibres.

questions.learning_objective: Relay site of T1-T2 preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head and neck

questions.title: Composition of the cell membrane
questions.question: The cell membrane is formed of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The membrane is not formed of a single layer of protein; protein is present as peripheral and integral molecules embedded in or attached to a separate lipid framework, not as the membrane's own structural layer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carbohydrate is present only as short chains attached to some membrane lipids and proteins on the outer face (the glycocalyx), not as a structural layer forming the membrane itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer -- two layers of phospholipid molecules arranged tail-to-tail, hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous environment on each side and hydrophobic tails facing each other in the interior -- with cholesterol, peripheral and integral proteins, and carbohydrate on its outer face completing the fluid mosaic structure. This double-layered lipid arrangement, not a single layer of any one component, is the membrane's defining structural framework, making 'lipid bilayer' the correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The membrane is a bilayer (two layers) of lipid, not a single layer; a single lipid layer would not be stable in an aqueous environment on both sides.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The membrane's structural framework is a lipid bilayer, not a protein bilayer; protein molecules are embedded in or attached to that lipid framework rather than forming a second bilayer of their own.

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p10

questions.title: True statement about the cell membrane
questions.question: Cell membranes:

options.A: Have a stable composition throughout the life of the cell
options.D: Contain peripheral proteins that act as receptors for hormones
options.E: Contain peripheral proteins that act as channels

explanations.A: Incorrect. Membrane composition is dynamic, not fixed; lipid and protein content shift with the cell's metabolic state, membrane turnover, and processes such as receptor recycling.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hydrophobic bilayer interior is a barrier to charged, water-soluble electrolytes (ions), which require specific channel or carrier proteins to cross rather than crossing freely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fat-soluble (lipophilic) substances dissolve readily in the membrane's hydrophobic lipid interior and cross it easily, the opposite of being impermeable to them.
explanations.D: Correct. The cell membrane's protein component includes both integral (transmembrane) and peripheral (attached non-covalently to one bilayer face) proteins. Peripheral proteins commonly function as receptors, enzymes or structural links to the cytoskeleton at either membrane face, so 'contain peripheral proteins that act as receptors for hormones' is a correct statement about the membrane, unlike the other four options, each of which misstates a membrane property (composition stability, electrolyte permeability, or fat-solubility handling).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Channel function is characteristically an integral (transmembrane) protein role, spanning the bilayer to form a continuous pore, rather than a peripheral (surface-attached) protein role.

questions.learning_objective: True statement about the cell membrane

questions.title: Feature of secondary active transport
questions.question: Concerning the secondary active transport:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Secondary active transport is an active, not passive, process, since it moves a solute against its own concentration gradient.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Direct ATP hydrolysis at the transport step is the definition of primary, not secondary, active transport.
explanations.C: Correct. Secondary active transport moves a solute against its concentration gradient by coupling that movement to the downhill flow of a second ion, typically Na+, through a shared carrier. The driving ion gradient is itself built up by a primary active transporter, such as the Na+/K+-ATPase, that directly consumes ATP, so secondary active transport uses cellular energy indirectly rather than hydrolysing ATP itself at the transport step. This indirect use of energy, borrowed from a previously established ion gradient, is exactly what defines secondary active transport and makes option C correct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secondary active transport moves the transported solute against its own concentration gradient (that is the 'active' part); it is the co-transported driving ion, not the transported solute itself, that moves with its gradient.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since options A, B and D are each false, 'all of the above' cannot be correct.

field_notes.mu: EOM Practice - Foundation 1 - Biochemistry and Physiology - Variant A.pdf, Biochemistry/Physiology continuation, Q from p10

questions.title: Nature of osmosis
questions.question: Osmosis:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Osmosis moves water down its own concentration gradient (from a region of lower solute/higher water concentration to higher solute/lower water concentration), not against a gradient.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Osmosis requires no carrier protein; water moves directly across the membrane (through the lipid bilayer and via aquaporin channels) rather than being carried by a transporter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osmosis requires no metabolic energy input; it is driven entirely by the water concentration gradient itself.
explanations.D: Correct. Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to one of higher solute concentration, driven by the water concentration gradient itself. It requires no carrier protein and no metabolic energy, making it a passive process, unlike the active transport of solutes. This passive, energy-independent, carrier-free character is exactly what makes option D the correct description of osmosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osmosis is specifically the movement of water (the solvent), not of an electrolyte (a dissolved solute); electrolyte movement across a membrane is a separate transport process.
